Bhagavadgītā
(‘Song of God’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā, popularly known as the Gītā, is one of the outstanding religious classics of the world. Hindus, irrespective of their sects and denomi-nations, cherish great reverence for this book. A ceremonial reading of the book or even a part there of, is believed to confer great religious merit.
The book itself, comprising eighteen chapters, forms an integral part of a much bigger work, the great epic Mahābhārata (vide Bhīṣmaparva, chapters 25 to 42). It is a poetical work in the form of a dialogue between Śrī कृष्ण and अर्जुन, on the battlefield of कुरुक्षेत्र. The setting of the battlefield contributes a dramatic element to the book and relates religion to the realities of life.
The greatness and the popularity of the Gītā can be attributed to several factors. It is part and parcel of the epic Mahābhārata which itself has been highly venerated as the fifth Veda (Pañcama-Veda). The teacher of the Gītā is Śrī कृष्ण, who is regarded by the Hindus as an अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of God Himself. An ideal friend, a great statesman, an invincible warrior, a wise preceptor and a योगि par excellence he harmonizes in his life the various conflicting activities of life. It is precisely this that makes him the fittest person to preach such a religio-spiritual classic. अर्जुन, the recipient of the teaching, though himself a great warrior, is a typical representative of the humans, easily liable to be upset or confused during periods of crisis. Hence, his predicament, very much represents ours, in a similar situation. The questions, doubts and misgivings he raises and the solutions that Śrī कृष्ण offers are not only relevant but also valid even today.
There is an additional reason too. The Hindu Vedāntic tradition has always regarded the प्रस्थानत्रय (the three foundational works) as its basis; and the Gītā is one of them, the other two being the उपनिषद्स् and the Brahmasūtras. That is why शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) and other ancient teachers have chosen to write commentaries on it.
Since the Gītā is an integral part of the epic Mahābhārata, its date and authorship are obviously the same as those of the epic itself. (See MAHĀBHĀRATA.) कृष्ण द्वैपायन, better known as वेदव्यास, is reputed to be its author. As per the Hindu oral traditions based on their notion of time as the yuga-system, the कुरुक्षेत्र war must have taken place during 3139 B.C. The dates given however by the modern historians and scholars (mostly of the West) vary from 1424 B.C. to 575 B.C. At the present stage of research, it may be difficult to clinch the issue on such chronological matters.
The widely accepted present text of the Gītā is based on the one chosen by शङ्कर, the earliest of the traditional commentators. It consists of 700 ślokas or verses spread over 18 chapters. The following is a brief summary of the book, arranged chapterwise.
Chapter 1 (Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga, 47 verses)
Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava hero, shaken by the prospect of killing the venerable भीष्म and the preceptor Droṇa, gets into a despondent mood at the start of the war. He describes the horrendous fallout of such wars, and lays down his arms refusing to fight.
Chapter 2 (Sāṅkhya-yoga, 72 verses)
Śrī कृष्ण, at first, admonishes अर्जुन for his unmanly and ignominious behaviour. This, however, falls on deaf ears. Hence he is obliged into giving a long philosophical discourse. Since the सोउल् inhabiting bodies, is immortal, one should not grieve over death and destruction. It is अर्जुन’s duty to fight this righteous war and win it or become a martyr if necessary, but never yield to unrighteousness. Work done as duty, in a spirit of detachment and for public good, ultimately leads to perfection. A perfect man (called ‘sthitaprajña’ here) is equanimous under all the vicissitudes of life.
Chapter 3 (Karmayoga, 43 verses)
Clearing अर्जुन’s doubts regarding the conflict between ज्ञान (knowledge), which envisages renunciation and कर्म (work, action) Śrī कृष्ण opines that the path of कर्म is easier and better for most people. Citing the example of ancient kings like जनक and of his own, he urges अर्जुन not to relinquish work, but to perform his duties without selfish motives.
Chapter 4 (Jñāna-yoga)
While reminiscing how कर्मयोग or the योग of action taught by him in the ancient days to Vivasvān and others got lost in course of time, Śrī कृष्ण reveals that he is God Himself come down to save धर्म or righteousness. He incarnates here out of his own will whenever धर्म declines, to put it on a firm foundation. He extols the greatness of ज्ञान or spiritual wisdom.
Chapter 5 (Karma-सṁन्यास-yoga, 29 verses)
Answering a question from अर्जुन whether कर्म-सṁन्यास (renunciation of action) or कर्मयोग (yoga of action) is better, Śrī कृष्ण avers that the latter is better for him. What is needed is equanimity while doing कर्म.
Chapter 6 (Dhyānayoga, 47 verses)
In this chapter Śrī कृष्ण describes the process of ध्यान or meditation. Place and posture suitable for meditation as also the methods of controlling the मिन्द् are graphically depicted.
Chapter 7 (Jñāna-विज्ञान-yoga, 30 verses)
Śrī कृष्ण as the Supreme Lord, has created the whole universe, drawing upon his twofold प्रकृति or nature. It is he that is holding together all beings and things. Only those that surrender themselves to him can transcend his māyā or power of delusion.
Chapter 8 (Akṣarabrahmayoga, 28 verses)
Śrī कृष्ण describes here how a person remembering Him at the moment of death attains Him. Repetition of प्रणव or Om at this juncture is a great help. He also mentions the two well-known paths—arcirādimārga and dhūmādimārga, the paths of light and smoke—which the jīvas or embodied beings take to after death.
Chapter 9 (Rājavidyā-rājaguhya-yoga, 34 verses)
Continuing the discourse, Śrī कृष्ण gives here the esoteric wisdom by which अर्जुन can get लिबेरतिओन्. He is everything in च्रेअतिओन्. If people can worship him with devotion, offering him even insigni-ficant things like a flower, or a leaf or water, he accepts them and blesses them. His devotee never perishes in life.
Chapter 10 (Vibhūtiyoga, 42 verses)
Śrī कृष्ण devotes this chapter almost entirely to the delineation of his vibhutis or divine manifestations. He is the best or the essence in all beings or things. The whole world has been supported by just a part of His glory.
Chapter 11 (Viśvarūpa-दर्शन-yoga, 55 verses)
At अर्जुन’s request whose curiosity has been roused, Śrī कृष्ण reveals his विश्वरूप or celestial form, after endowing him with a divine sight. Awed by it, अर्जुन offers his prayers and obeisance. Śrī कृष्ण withdraws the विश्वरूप and declares that it can be seen only by those who have intense devotion.
Chapter 12 (Bhaktiyoga, 20 verses)
In this chapter, Śrī कृष्ण declares that even though contemplation on the अव्यक्त or the Unmanifest leads to the same result as devotion to him, the latter path is better. He advises अर्जुन to cultivate devotion to him. Towards the end, the characteristics of a भक्त or an ideal devotee are delineated.
Chapter 13 (Kṣetra-क्षेत्रज्ञ-yoga, 34 verses)
The body is the क्षेत्र or the field. The Self is the क्षेत्रज्ञ or the knower of the field. These two are described in this chapter. This is followed by descriptions of ज्ञान (knowledge), jñeya (that which is to be known, viz., ब्रह्मन्), प्रकृति (nature) and पुरुष (the Self or क्षेत्रज्ञ). Those who can intuit the difference between the last two, will attain ब्रह्मन्.
Chapter 14 (Guṇatraya-vibhāga-yoga, 27 verses)
Prakṛti or nature from which च्रेअतिओन् proceeds, prodded by the Lord (Śrī कृष्ण), comprises the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. There is a detailed description of these guṇas and also that of the गुणातीत or the person who has transcen-ded them.
Chapter 15 (Puruṣottama-yoga, 20 verses)
In this chapter Śrī कृष्ण describes सṁसार or the created world as an inverted tree with its roots above, in ब्रह्मन् or Purāṇa-पुरुष, the Primeval Being. By taking refuge in Him, this tree can be cut resulting in लिबेरतिओन्. There is also a description of transmigration of the जीव, the bound सोउल्. Śrī कृष्ण also states that He is the power that sustains the world and the living beings. He is the पुरुषोत्तम or the Best of beings.
Chapter 16 (Daivāsura-sampad-vibhāga-yoga, 24 verses)
Śrī कृष्ण delineates here those traits of character (sampat) that make a person divine (daivī) or demoniac (āsurī). He assures अर्जुन that he belongs to the divine group but urges him to avoid the three gateways to हेल्ल्: lust, anger and greed.
Chapter 17 (Śraddhātraya-vibhāga-yoga, 28 verses)
This chapter contains interesting des-criptions of श्रद्धा (faith), आहार (food), यज्ञ (sacrifices), तपस् (austerity) and दान (gifts), all being divided into three categories according to the three guṇas. Śrī कृष्ण also gives the aphorism ‘Oṁ tat sat,’ a designation for ब्रह्मन्, which can act as a magic formula to correct the deficiencies in religious acts.
Chapter 18 (Mokṣa-सṁन्यास-yoga) 78 verses)
This is the last and the longest chapter dealing with several miscellaneous topics like त्याग and सṁन्यास (renunci-ation), ज्ञान (knowledge), कर्म (action) and kartā (doer) classified as per the three guṇas. There is also the mention of the society being divided into four varṇas or groups, according to nature and vocation. Finally Śrī कृष्ण advises अर्जुन to totally surrender himself to Him, with the promise of freeing him from all sins. अर्जुन, with his delusion destroyed by this wonderful discourse vows to fight in obedience to his command.
The Philosophy of the Bhagavadgītā
The Indian philosophical systems, known as darśanas, generally treat their subject under four major headings: the Cause of the universe; च्रेअतिओन् or evolution of the universe; nature of the individual सोउल्; the goal of human life and the means of achieving it. Though the Bhagavadgītā is not a systematic treatise on philosophy it is possible to deal with its subject matter under these headings. It may not be out of place to mention here that the colophon given at the end of each chapter of the Gītā viz., Upaniṣad, ब्रह्मविद्या and Yogaśāstra, reflects its contents very well. It is an ‘Upaniṣad’ or esoteric wisdom given by the teacher to a disciple on request. It is ‘Brahmavidyā’ since it deals with ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute. It is ‘Yogaśāstra’ since it describes योग or practical disciplines that help an aspirant to attain spiritual wisdom, the goal of life.
Śrī कृष्ण has been venerated and worshipped as God Himself, come down as a human being, to save mankind and re-direct it in the path of धर्म or righteousness. In the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata, as also in the Gītā itself, Śrī कृष्ण often identified himself with God and speaks with indisputable authority. While studying the philosophy of the Gītā, it is necessary to keep this fact in मिन्द्.
The Gītā compares the created universe to an inverted tree with its roots above, established in God (15.1-4). The more popular view of the mythological lore that ब्रह्मा (the four-faced Creator) creates the world during his ‘day’ and withdraws it into himself during ‘night,’ is also referred to (8.17-19). The various terms used to indicate the Supreme or God are: परब्रह्मन् (13.12), परमात्मन् (13.22, 31), उत्तमपुरुष or पुरुषोत्तम (15.17-19), ईश्वर (15.17; 18.61), क्षेत्रज्ञ (13.2) and परमेश्वर (13.27).
God has a twofold प्रकृति or nature. The aparā or the lower one is insentient and comprises these eight: the five elements like earth and water, मनस् (mind), बुद्धि (intellect) and अहङ्कार (egoism). The parā or the higher one consists of the innumerable jīvas or souls. च्रेअतिओन् proceeds out of the combination of these two. It is under His direction that प्रकृति gives birth to all beings and things. He is the sole origin and place of dissolution of this universe (7.4-6; 9.7). The whole universe is supported by Him even as the beads of a necklace are supported by the string on which they are strung (7.7). As अव्यक्त or the Unmanifest, He has pervaded the whole universe (9.4). That is why He is the essence of all, in this च्रेअतिओन् (10.41).
God is not only transcendent and immanent (18.61), he can also incarnate himself as a human being, whenever धर्म or righteousness declines, in order to restore its balance. He does it out of his own free will. By his māyā-power, and subjugating his प्रकृति, he creates a body for himself (4.6-8).
As इन्चर्नतिओन्, the personal aspect of the Impersonal, God is more easily approachable through devotion (9.26). He responds in whatever way people approach him (4.11; 7.21-23). His devotee never gets perished (9.31). Those who surrender to him will easily cross over māyā (the delusive power of God), which is otherwise impossible to cross (7.14). He takes over their entire responsibility even here in this world (9.22). That is why He constantly urges अर्जुन to cultivate devotion to him and surrender to him (9.34; 11.55; 18.65, 66).
The जीव or the individual सोउल् is an important aspect of this च्रेअतिओन्. He is a part of God (15.7). He is the higher aspect of his nature, पराप्रकृति (7.5). He is essentially unborn, indestructible and eternal (2.17-25). He takes on bodies like wearing garments and then discards them, to take new ones (2.22). While doing so he draws to himself the five sense-organs and the मिन्द् from the aparā प्रकृति or the lower प्रकृति (7.4, 5) and transmigrates with them. He is deluded by अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे which covers ज्ञान or know-ledge (5.15).
The goal of life is to reach the Lord’s Abode from which there is no return to this mundane existence (8.16; 5.17; 15.6). This state has been variously called as brahma-निर्वाण (dissolution into Brahman—2.72; 5.24), brāhmīsthiti (being established in Brahman—2.72), saṁsiddhi (perfection—8.15; 18.45), parāgati (highest state—6.45; 8.13, 21; 9.32; 13.28; 16.22) and attaining Śrī कृष्ण Himself (4.9, 10; 5.29; 7.3, 18, 23, 30; 8.5, 7, 14, 15, 16; 9.28, 34; 10.10; 11.55; 12.4, 9; 18.55). The ancient Upaniṣadic idea of the जीव reaching ब्रह्मलोक (Abode of ब्रह्मा) by the अर्चिरादि-मार्ग or the path of light, has also been mentioned by the Gītā (8.24-26).
Since it is अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे that is responsible for transmigration, it can be erased only by ज्ञान or spiritual wisdom which alone can accomplish it (4.35-39; 5.16, 17).
Acquisition of ज्ञान has to be preceded by spiritual disciplines that help in purifying the मिन्द्. इन्द्रियनिग्रह or control of sense-organs is one of the most important disciplines referred to (2.58, 60, 61, 64, 68; 3.34, 41; 5.22, 23; 6.4, 24; 12.4). तपस् or austerity (16.1; 17.14-16; 18.5) and other disciplines including the performance of one’s duties with the right attitude have also been recommended. But devotion to the Lord and surrendering to him have been highly extolled (7.21; 8.10, 22; 9.14, 26, 29, 31; 11.54; 12.17, 20; 13.10; 14.26; 18.55).
There are three beautiful descriptions of the perfect being, who has reached the final goal of life: the स्थितप्रज्ञ or the man of steady wisdom (2.55-72), the भक्त or the devotee (12.13-20) and the गुणातीत or one who has transcended the three guṇas (14.22-27).
The स्थितप्रज्ञ (man of steady wisdom) is bereft of all desires. He is unmoved by the pairs of opposites like pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion. He is capable of withdrawing his sense-organs from the sense-objects effortlessly. He is the supreme master of himself. He can wield his sense-organs among the sense-objects without being affected by them. He is ever awake to the आत्मन्, the reality within himself. He is free from egoism and possessiveness, and hence ever filled with peace. This state is called brāhmīsthiti; the state of being established in ब्रह्मन्.
The भक्त or the ideal devotee who is ever dear to God, is free from inimical thoughts towards all beings. He has nothing but friendliness and compassion for them. He has neither egoism nor attachment. He is ever equanimous and contented. Having controlled the senses and the मिन्द्, he has totally dedicated them to God, out of devotion. He is never upset by the people nor are they agitated by him. Bereft of desires, pure to the core and expert in the field of work, he has yet renounced all selfish works. Deeply devo-ted to God, indifferent to praise and blame, unaffected by the vagaries of the weather and having no fixed place for dwelling, the भक्त is extremely dear to the Lord.
The गुणातीत (who is beyond the three guṇas) is ever unaffected by the experiences brought about by the three guṇas, like knowledge or happiness or delusion. He knows that the guṇas as the senses act upon the guṇas as objects and that he as the Self is beyond them. He looks upon happiness and misery, wealth and worthless objects, praise and blame with equipoise. He never undertakes desire-motivated actions, but ever serves God through devotion.
Special Contribution of the गीता to Indian Philosophical Thought
Though the Gītā has been reputed to contain the essence of the teachings of the उपनिषद्स् and is considered to be one of the three basic scriptures of Vedānta (prasthānatraya) there is no gainsaying the fact that it has charted new avenues in the Indian philosophical literature, previously unknown or unexpressed. The work presents us with three original doctrines: a. The doctrine of niṣkāma-कर्म-योग (or the योग of desireless action), with the allied concepts of स्वधर्म and लोक-saṅgraha; b. The doctrine of integral योग as a comprehensive mode of sādhanā (or spiritual discipline); and c. The doctrine of अवतार (descent of God into the human form or the theory of इन्चर्नतिओन् of God.)
a. The Doctrine of Niṣkāmakarmayoga:
At the time of Śrī कृष्ण, two major streams of thought, resulting in two different views and ways of life existed. On one side was the philosophy of अभ्युदय or worldly well-being with its inordinate emphasis on yajñas and yāgas, sacrificial rites and rituals, by which one could get everything in life, here and hereafter. Since this involved a lot of time, energy and money, and since the results were considered petty, the reaction came in the form of the doctrine of niśśreyasa or the highest good, put forward by the sages of the उपनिषद्स्, who advocated a life of renunciation of all actions except those needed for the bare sustenance of life, coupled with mendicancy and contem-plation on the आत्मन् (the Self) within.
By their very nature these two views and ways were restricted to the ब्राह्मण-क्षत्त्रिय combine, at least, to the more affluent and the more rigorous amongst them. As a result, the majority of the people were left in the lurch, though imbued with higher spiritual aspirations. It is here that Śrī कृष्ण’s doctrine of niṣkāma-कर्म-योग becomes relevant and extremely useful.
Being a wise and sensible leader, Śrī कृष्ण accepts the tradition of sacrifices as it existed then, but shows the way to transform it or even transcend it. Since प्रजापति (Father of beings) created the system of यज्ञ or sacrifice as a link between human beings and gods, they are expected to prosper only by mutual help and cooperation (3.10, 11). But a यज्ञ or sacrifice need not be only that done in a duly consecrated fire. Any act of an indi-vidual, involving the sacrifice of selfishness and done for the public good can also be a यज्ञ (vide 4.25-30).
After defining सṁन्यास as the renunciation of all kāmya-karmas or desire-motivated actions, and त्याग as the abandonment of sarvakarmaphala or the fruits of all actions (18.21), Śrī कृष्ण rules out the renunciation of actions like यज्ञ (sacrificial rites), दान (giving gifts) and तपस् (austerity) since they purify the मिन्द् (18.5). Even they are to be performed without attachment and the desire for fruits, as a matter of duty. What really binds one is not work itself, but the selfish desire for its fruits (vide 9.20, 21). Since work is inevitable for an embodied being (3.5,8; 18.11) it is better to accept the fact gracefully and perform it with self-control (3.7), as a यज्ञ or sacrifice (3.9) and giving up the desire for the fruits thereof (3.19; 12.11). One who performs actions thus is both a saṁnyāsi and a योगि (6.1). Alternatively, one can perform actions for the sake of God and offer the fruits thereof (3.19; 12.11). One who performs actions thus is both a saṁnyāsi and a योगि (6.1). Alternatively, one can perform actions for the sake of God and offer the fruits also to him (12.6,10, 11; 11.55; 5.10-12). It is necessary to perform actions even from the standpoint of लोकसङ्ग्रह or guiding the people on the right path (3.20, 25) which is the bounden duty of the leaders of the society.
Work done in the right spirit, thus, can also lead to मोक्ष (liberation or perfection). It is in no way less effective than ज्ञान or knowledge. Many a great one in the past, like जनक, attained perfection through the path of action alone (3.19, 20; 4.15, 23, 41; 5.5, 6, 12; 8.7; 9.27, 28; 12.12; 18.45, 46, 56). Not only that, such persons, including Śrī कृष्ण himself, continued to live in the society and work, to set an example to the unenlightened ones, as to perfection in work, which also will lead to beatitude (3.21-26).
Arjuna was a sincere seeker of spiritual wisdom. He was not interested in sakāma-कर्म or desire-motivated actions. However, he was not qualified to tread the path of ज्ञान or knowledge which entails renunciation of all actions. That is why Śrī कृष्ण declares that अर्जुन has the competence only to work; and not to renouncing it; but he should do so without reference to the fruits thereof (2.47).
Closely associated with this, is the idea of ‘svadharma’, ‘dharma’ or duties that are ‘sva’ or one’s own, accruing to one by one’s nature and nurture, and, ordained by the scriptures. It goes without saying that ‘svadharma’ must be ‘dharma’ (righteousness) first. Such स्वधर्म should never be abandoned. If performed, it brings in great good; if abandoned, sin (2.31-33). However imperfect it may appear, it is far better to die performing it than to do paradharma or someone else’s धर्म which is unsuitable (3.35). One who acts according to स्वधर्म will never be tainted by its effects (18.47). There is no doubt that the performance of स्वधर्म in the right spirit will lead to perfection (18.45, 46).
b. The Doctrine of Integral योग:
As already stated, the colophon of the Gītā calls it as a ‘yogaśāstra.’ ‘Yoga’ is a technical term which means union with God as also the spiritual discipline that leads to such union.
Though योग is one, taking into consideration the different types of human mind—the active, the philosophical, the emotional and the psychic—it has branched off into four paths: कर्मयोग, the path of work for the active:, ज्ञान-योग, the path of knowledge, for the philo-sophical; भक्तियोग, the path of devotion, for the emotional; and, राजयोग, the path of psychic control for the psychic. Each of these yogas opens upon the infinite horizon of Truth and effects union with God. The Gītā describes them all.
Śrī कृष्ण has used the word ‘yoga’ in several senses. For instance, it is कर्मयोग that is meant in 2.48, 50 and 6.2. However, in 6.12 and 15 it is राजयोग that is indicated. In 5.8 the word ‘yukta’ has been used to signify the jñānayogi. Again, it is the bhaktiyogi that is implied by the word ‘nityayukta’ in 8.14.
Keeping in मिन्द् the fact that Śrī कृष्ण has taught all the four yogas to one and the same person, अर्जुन, urging him to follow them, it can be safely concluded that the योग of the Gītā is a comprehensive spiritual discipline integra-ting into itself all the four aspects. However, since अर्जुन’s svabhāva or nature was such that कर्मयोग was better suited to him, Śrī कृष्ण relentlessly urges him to fight (2.18; 3.30; 11.34).
The inference is obvious: The Gītā urges an aspirant to practise a balanced combination of all the four yogas, keeping that योग which suits one’s nature better, as the main discipline and adding the others too in right proportion. Since no human being has only one of the four faculties mentioned earlier, but all the four, though in varying proportions, this deduction is reasonable.
c. The Doctrine of अवतार:
The doctrine of अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of God is another, original contribution of the Gītā to Indian philosophical and religious literature. The अवतार concept is perhaps suggested in the Ṛgveda (3.53.8; 6.47.18) itself. Some of the avatāras mentioned in the पुराणस् in the lists of दशावतारस् (ten incarnations of विष्णु) are met with in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1.-6; 1.2.5.1). However, it is only here in the Gītā, that the concept is more definite and clear.
When Śrī कृष्ण mentions that the योग which he taught to Vivasvān (Sun-god) and transmitted by him to मनु was lost in course of time, अर्जुन naturally questions him out of unbelief how a contemporary person like him could have taught a person who lived in hoary antiquity (4.1-4). It is then that Śrī कृष्ण reveals the truth of both of them passing through many births. Whereas अर्जुन underwent those births helplessly due to prārabdha कर्म (residual कर्म, responsible for rebirth) and did not know about them, Śrī कृष्ण being the Supreme Lord himself, voluntarily and willingly accepted these births for a higher purpose.
It is धर्म or righteousness that is the principle regulating the smooth working of the created world. Since the created world is a product of the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and tamas—which are constantly in a state of flux, it is but natural that each one of them gets the upper hand periodically. Whenever सत्त्व goes down and रजस् or तमस् comes up, धर्म declines and अधर्म (evil) gets the upper hand. At such critical periods of human history, the Supreme Lord decides to incar-nate himself in a human frame to restore the balance. Though he is unborn, eternal and the Lord of all beings, he can and does ‘come down’ (avatāra = coming down) by taking recourse to his māyā-power (also called प्रकृति or nature) (4.6, 7). The primary purpose of the अवतार is धर्म-saṁsthāpana or establishing धर्म on a firm foundation. In the process, if need be, He will destroy or chastise the wicked and thereby protect the good (4.8).
This descent of the Divine into the human frame can take place anywhere, anytime, the sole condition being the decline of धर्म and the ascent of अधर्म (4.7) to the extent of rendering the good people absolutely helpless, and at the mercy of the evil ones.
There is an added assurance given by Śrī कृष्ण that one who is able to understand the significance of his birth and work as an अवतार, will attain लिबेरतिओन् (4.9).
Of course, in a number of places, he urges अर्जुन to cultivate devotion to him, to meditate upon him and to work for him (9.34; 11.55; 18.65), the finale being the command to surrender totally to him, with the pledge to free him from all sins (18.66).
Commentaries
Being a part of the प्रस्थानत्रय and thus accorded a very high place in the religio-philosophical tradition of India, the Gītā has attracted the attention of several ancient and medieval teachers who have written commentaries and glosses on it in Sanskrit. In the Advaita Vedānta tradition शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) comes first. In fact, his is the earliest of the extant commentaries. Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137), Madhva (A. D. 1197-1276), निम्बार्क (12th century A. D.) and वल्लभ (A. D. 1473-1531) are the other great ācāryas or teachers who have written commentaries on the Gītā. आनन्दगिरि (A. D. 1200), वेदान्त देशिक (A. D. 1268-1370) and जयतीर्थ (13th century A. D.) have written glosses on the commentaries of शङ्कर, Rāmānuja and Madhva respec-tively. Mention may also be made of the commentaries of Śrīdhara (15th century A. D.), Madhusūdana (A. D. 1525-1632) and Rāghavendra (A. D. 1598-1671) who have made some original contributions to the गीता literature.
Conclusion
The Bhagavadgītā is one of the most translated religious classics of the world. The beauty and the sublimity of the work, its eternal relevance to the problems of human life and its universal approach that helps us view the whole च्रेअतिओन् as one, may have prompted the scholars to under-take the task of translating it as a labour of love.
Though part of the great epic Mahā-bhārata, it can as well stand on its own as an independent work. Though taught on the battlefield of कुरुक्षेत्र, urging अर्जुन to fight, it has nothing to do with wars or battles or bloodshed, but only with the discharging of one’s sacred duties of life, however unpleasant they may be. Though given by Śrī कृष्ण to अर्जुन in the days of yore, its declarations like, ‘Remember Me and fight!’ (8.7) can help and inspire anyone of us, beleaguered with serious problems of life, even now. Though recognizing multiplicity here, its principle of unity in diversity as signified by the Viśavarūpa or the Cosmic Form (11.9-13) and the underlying divinity as taught in 7.7, help us to cultivate a holistic approach to the universe of which ecological balance too is only a small aspect.
If the Mahābhārata can claim to be an encyclopaedia of Hindu religion and culture, the Bhagavadgītā can as well claim to be its quintessence.

Bhagavatī
------------------------------------------
The theistic systems of Hindu philo-sophy and the cults based on them use the general term ‘Bhagavān’ to denote God since He possesses ‘bhaga’ or the six blessed qualities of ज्ञान (knowledge), ऐश्वर्य (lordship) and so on, in abundance. His power, conceived as His consort, is called ‘Bhagavatī; same as शक्ति or देवी.
Though this word can apply to any goddess or female deity, it is almost invariably used to denote पार्वती and her several aspects.
In the heart of the town Chengannur (in the Alleppy district of Kerala State) is situated a well-known temple of a goddess known as भगवती. According to the local legend, शिव and पार्वती presented themselves before the sage अगस्त्य, at the time of their मर्रिअगे and settled down there. While residing there, the देवी had her menses, thus forcing the couple to stay back till the periods were over and the purificatory bath gone through. Even today, the devotees believe that the goddess Bhagavatī—whose image is cast in pañcaloha or an alloy of five metals—has her periods. The cella is kept closed for three days during such periods. On the fourth day there is a bathing ritual, conducted in the nearby river पम्पा.
Stories abound about the sceptics who had derided this phenomenon, having incurred the wrath of the deity and come to grief.
The temple, sprawling over a six-acre plot, is a massive structure. The image of the deity faces west. After the original icon was damaged by fire, it was replaced by a pañcaloha idol. It is a beautiful image, about 60 cms. in height and has two hands in the varada (boon-giving) and abhaya (granting protection) poses.
There is also a shrine for शिव and the लिङ्ग is of the svayambhū (self-manifested) type. Subsidiary shrines dedicated to गणेश and Caṇḍeśa located inside the complex, and temples of शास्ता and कृष्ण, a little away, are the other attractions. A giant peepul tree on the western side is said to be endowed with the miraculous power of curing those possessed by evil spirits.
The original temple might have been built by the Cerman dynasty (9th to 12th cent.). It was renovated later, though this renovation has not been completed.

Bhāgavata-dharma
(‘The भागवत Religion’)
------------------------------------------
Bhakti or love of God is a very ancient religious sentiment. Its origin can be traced even to the Ṛgveda (1.156.3; 8.98.11). It appears like a flash of lightning in the उपनिषद्स् (vide Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.23; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23). By the time of the epics and the पुराणस् it has grown to voluminous proportions.
Gradually भक्ति was developed into a doctrine or a religion or even a philosophy. This has been christened as ‘Bhāgavata-धर्म.’ The term ‘Bhāgavata-धर्म’ has been derived from the word ‘Bhagavat’ or God, endowed with ‘bhaga’ or the six divine attributes of ऐश्वर्य (lordship), धर्म (righteousness), yaśas (celebrity), śrī (wealth and splendour), ज्ञान (knowledge) and वैराग्य (detachment). Since this God is identified with नारायण, this religion is also called ‘Nārāyaṇīya-धर्म.’ It was also called ‘Sātvata-mata’ since it was current among the people of the ‘satvat’ tribe to which कृष्ण belonged. As it teaches ekānta-भक्ति or single-minded devotion, it has come to be known as ‘Ekāntika or Aikāntika mata.’ Other names of this system are: Pāñcarātra mata (religion as taught in the Pāñcarātra Āgamas) and Vaiṣṇava-धर्म (religion of the followers of विष्णु).
The Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahā-bhārata (Śāntiparva ch. 334 onwards), Viṣṇupurāṇa, भगवद्गीता, भागवत, पाञ्चरात्र आगमस्, Bhaktisūtras of शाण्डिल्य and Nārada—these are the sources of the भागवत-धर्म.
Not being satisfied with the impersonal ब्रह्मन् of the उपनिषद्स्, the भागवत religion has converted it into the Personal God. ईश्वर, Mahāviṣṇu, नारायण and कृष्ण-वासुदेव are some of the names most commonly used with respect of him. He cannot be apprehended by the senses nor by लोगिच्. Śrutis or scriptures, at best, point towards him. His grace is the supreme factor in realizing him. Ekānta-भक्ति or single-minded devotion is the only mode by which his grace can be obtained and he can be apprehended. Though He is ‘sarvatantra-svatantra’ or supremely independent, actually it is not so! He is always ‘bhakta-parādhīna’ or subject to the will of the devotees! He is ever fond of those that are devoted to him and reveals himself to them. प्रपत्ति or शरणागति (complete resignation) is another means of attaining him.
The Caturvyūha doctrine is another speciality of this भागवत-धर्म. The four व्यूहस् or emanations of the Lord विष्णु are: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध. They are different aspects of manifestation of the six qualities known as ‘bhaga’ mentioned earlier. While वासुदेव has all the six qualities in full measure, the other three have two each in greater measure than the others.
Followers of the भागवत-धर्म are called ‘bhāgavatas.’
See also BHĀGAVATA and PĀÑCARĀTRA ĀGAMAS.

Bhagavanta-bhāskara
------------------------------------------
The Hindu way of life has been influenced, to a very large extent, by the धर्मशास्त्रस्. These धर्मशास्त्रस्, chronologically speaking, fall into three categories:
The धर्मसूत्रस् and the मनुस्मृति (6th century B.C. to the beginning of the Christian era);
The versified smṛtis (upto A.D. 800);
The commentaries and निबन्धस् or digests (A.D. 800-1800).
One of the well-known निबन्धस् or digests is the Bhagavanta-bhāskara of नीलकण्ठ (17th century), a son of Śaṅkarabhaṭṭa, who was a profound scholar of Mīmāṁsā. नीलकण्ठ composed this encyclopaedic work of religious and civil law, in honour of his patron Bhagavantadeva, a Bundella chieftain of the Sengara clan that ruled at Bareha, near the confluence of the rivers Jumna (Yamunā) and Chambal.
This work has been divided into 12 sections called ‘mayūkhas’ (or ‘rays’), the topics dealt with being: saṁskāra (sacraments), आचार (personal conduct), kāla (time), śrāddha (afterdeath ceremonies), नीति (ethics), vyavahāra (social behaviour), दान (gifts), उत्सर्ग (dedication for public benefit), pratiṣṭhā (foundation of temples for public good), प्रायश्चित्त (expiations for sins), शुद्धि (purificatory rites) and śānti (propitiatory rites).
The rules given in this work are considered as a great authority in certain parts of India even now.
See also NIBANDHAS.

Bhagīratha
------------------------------------------
The word ‘bhagīratha-prayatna’ often used in Indian literature for Herculean efforts in any field, owes its origin to the king भगीरथ, the son of दिलीप of the इक्ष्वाकु race, ruling in अयोध्या for several generations.
The Sāgaras, 60,000 sons of the सगर, an ancestor of भगीरथ, had been reduced to ashes by the wrath of the sage कपिल. The only way of their spiritual redemption was to bring the river गङ्गा from the svargaloka or हेअवेन्, and make its waters flow over these ashes. Though successive kings tried to do it, they failed. Finally, it was भगीरथ who succeeded in doing so.
He performed very severe austerities to please ब्रह्मा, the Creator, who appeared before him and advised him to solicit the help of शिव who alone could arrest the torrential flow of the river गङ्गा and slow her down. भगीरथ did तपस् or penance once again and appeased शिव who agreed to do so. Then, at the behest of ब्रह्मा and the request of the king भगीरथ, गङ्गा descended on to शिव’s जटा or matted hair, emerged as a stream, followed the king right up to the पाताल or the nether world and flowed over the ashes, thus redeeming the Sāgaras.
Since भगीरथ brought the river गङ्गा down to this earth, it has come to be known as the ‘Bhāgīrathī.’
Some mythological works say that भगीरथ was the son of अṁशुमान्, the grandson of सगर.
See also GAṄGĀ.

Bhaga
------------------------------------------
Bhaga is one of the twelve Ādityas (solar deities of the वेदस्) born to कश्यप प्रजापति and his wife अदिति.
According to another view he is classed among the eleven Rudras.
He is said to be the lord of the month पुष्य (January-February). It is quite likely that the twelve Ādityas are the twelve aspects of the sun spread over the twelve months and the aspect connected with the month पुष्य is named भग.
There was one भग in the sacrificial assembly of दक्ष प्रजापति. He too like others was subjected to the wrath of वीरभद्र, the terrible emissary of शिव, and lost his eyes.
The word भग represents the group of six guṇas or blessed qualities: ऐश्वर्य (lordship), धर्म (righteousness), yaśas (renown), śrī (splendour), ज्ञान (know-ledge) and वैराग्य (detachment). One who possesses these in abundance is ‘Bhagavān.’ The term is generally applied to God; and even to sages and prophets. When applied to a goddess it becomes ‘Bhagavatī.’
Sometimes these six guṇas are listed in a slightly different way: ज्ञान, ऐश्वर्य, शक्ति (ability), बल (strength), vīrya (viri-lity) and तेजस् (splendour). They are considered as the material or instruments of śuddhasṛṣṭi or pure च्रेअतिओन्. They also play a part in the manifestation of व्यूहस् or emanations from God वासुदेव viz., सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध.

Bhāgīrathī
(‘connected with भगीरथ’)
------------------------------------------
One of the several names of the river गङ्गा is भागीरथी,since it was brought from हेअवेन् to this earth by the king भगीरथ.
See BHAGĪRATHA and GAṄGĀ.

Bhāgyasūkta
(‘hymn [requesting for] wealth and well-being’)
------------------------------------------
It is but natural for every human being to desire for wealth and well-being in this world. When he finds that he cannot get what he wants by his limited efforts alone, he may be tempted to try unethical means. Intuiting such a possibility, our ṛṣis have provided the aspirants with appropriate prayers to God to get what they want. The Bhāgyasūkta may be classed among such prayers.
It occurs in two places: The Ṛgveda (7.3.41) and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (2.8.9).
According to the Ṛgvedic version, वसिष्ठ is the ṛṣi (the sage to whom it was revealed) and भग is the chief devatā or deity. The छन्दस् or metre is जगती and triṣṭubh.
A brief summary of its contents may now be attempted here:
We invoke the various Vedic gods like अग्नि, इन्द्र, भग, मित्र, वरुण, रुद्र and others at this hour of dawn.
(Bhaga is the chief deity of this सूक्त. He is the giver or distributor of all the good things of life.)
One who wants wealth—whether he is poor or even a king—can pray for it from भग, the powerful sustainer of this world.
O भग! You, the possessor of true wealth, listen to our prayer and grant us boons in the form of cattle, horses, children and relatives.
May we have भग for our lord, at all times of day.
O gods! May भग only be the possessor of opulence. O भग, who is invoked by all, you be our guide.
May the gods उषस् (deities of dawn), bring भग, the giver of wealth, to us for our sacrifice.
May the auspicious gods of dawn who give rains, bless us with horses, cows, and heroic sons.
The Ṛgvidhāna (2.25) of शौनक (circa 500 B. C.) declares that those who are suffering from diseases as also those who want to enter a new होउसे, should repeat this सूक्त as a prayer.
Some texts have an extra verse at the end. Its meaning is—‘O अग्नि! One who wants me to be deprived of wealth, you please deprive him of his wealth!’
See also BHAGA.

Bhāgavata
(‘related to Bhagavat or God’)
------------------------------------------
INTRODUCTION
Rāma and कृष्ण (the most prominent of the incarnations of विष्णु-नारायण), शिव and देवी, form the four main pillars upon which the edifice of Hindu theism rests. The two epics, Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, as also the vast paurāṇika literature, form the basis for the various cults and sects that have woven the texture of the variegated Hindu fabric. Among the various पुराणस्, however, it is the Bhāgavata that has earned a pre-eminent place for itself, not only for its philosophical content and devotional fervour but also for its exquisite literary beauty. Though basically a text of the भागवत school preaching the विष्णु-नारायण-कृष्ण cult, it is remarkably catholic in its outlook and has successfully harmonized Advaita philosophy as also the Śaiva cults with its basic tenets. While a study of this work is definitely fascinating and highly rewarding, it has also been considered as a test of one’s scholarship.
PURĀṆAS
The Bhāgavata has been classed among the पुराणस्. Hence a few words about them will not be out of place here. Since early Vedic literature like the Atharvaveda, शतपथ ब्राह्मण, Gopatha Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad mention the word purāṇa (in singular), it may be inferred that the purāṇa was a branch of Vedic learning. The earliest beginnings of the purāṇa literature have been traced to the Pāri-plava Ākhyānas or narrations, commemorating the genealogies of great kingly lines and allied subjects, recited during periods of intervals in sacrifices. In course of time, recitation of the purāṇa seems to have been relegated to the sūtas (members of a mixed caste) since it was not integral to the sacrifices. This bifurcation helped in the development of a number of पुराणस् and उपपुराणस् (minor पुराणस्) under the leadership of eminent sūtas like लोमहर्षण who was a disciple of व्यास. It is very likely that व्यास compiled the original Purāṇa-saṁhitā which was expanded and divided by लोमहर्षण and his disciples, resulting in course of time, in eighteen पुराणस् and eighteen उपपुराणस् as extant now. In the light of this, it is understandable how व्यास has been taken to be the author of all these पुराणस् and उपपुराणस्.
There has been a controversy whether the ‘Bhāgavata’ included in the list of the eighteen पुराणस् (also called sometimes, as mahāpurāṇas) is Devībhāgavata or this (Viṣṇu) Bhāgavata. Many scholars opine in favour of the latter.
DATE AND AUTHORSHIP
With several unknown or variable factors involved, fixing the dates of ancient Hindu scriptures, has always been a difficult exercise. The Bhāgavata is no exception to this. The internal evidence of the work, viz., शुक teaching it to king परीक्षित्, takes the date to the beginning of the कलि-yuga, around 3000 B.C. This is the opinion of the orthodox groups. Another view, that poet बोपदेव (13th cent.) was the author, has been thoroughly discounted by several scholars. A few are of the conviction that the core of the purāṇa is very old. However, it was given the shape of a महापुराण in the early Christian era and further expanded by the Tamil saints of South India, contemporaneous with the आऌवार्स् (5th-8th cent. A. D.) Thus, there has been a three-phase development of the text.
Though tradition ascribes the authorship to the sage वेदव्यास, who was the author of the core of the work, those responsible for the second and third phases of development have remained unknown.
SYNOPSIS OF THE CONTENTS
The Bhāgavata as available today, has been divided into 12 skandhas or books, further divided into 335 adhyāyas or chapters, containing in all, a little more than 14,000 ślokas or verses. However, tradition has always put it at 18,000 verses.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be given here:
First Skandha (19 chapters, 809 verses)
This skandha, though introductory in form, is the final section added to complete the narration of कृष्ण’s story and glory. In this sense, it may perhaps be considered as a supplement to the tenth skandha. The famous line ‘Kṛṣṇastu भगवान् svayam’ occurring here (3.28) also signifies the finale to the development of the भागवत literature. It also describes how the Bhāgavata came to be written.
After an introduction through the story of शौनक and other sages performing a Sattra-याग (a long-drawn fire sacrifice), the book expatiates the glory of the भागवत धर्म or the life of devotion to the Lord, which can be cultivated through the study of the Bhāgavata and the teachings of कृष्ण who lives in it. This is followed by a narration of how the Bhāgavata came to be composed by व्यास, on the advice of the sage नारद, to get peace of मिन्द्.
The book covers the last part of the story of the Pāṇḍavas including the incident of king परीक्षित् being cursed by a sage, to die of snake-bite. When the king has resigned himself to his fate, the sage शुक, the son of व्यास, arrives there and starts narrating the story of the Bhāgavata for his spiritual good.
Second Skandha (10 chapters, 391 verses)
Smallest of the twelve skandhas, this book may probably be the nucleus of the original Bhāgavata.
Meditation on the Virāṭpuruṣa or the Cosmic Divinity, the ascent of the सोउल् of योगि to the ब्रह्मलोक, a description of the devotion to the Lord, शुक’s prayer to the Supreme Lord, glory of Lord नारायण and his incarnations as also a brief account of the cosmic theories and theological doctrines of Bhāgavata form the subject-matter of this skandha.
The well-known Catuśślokī-Bhāga-vata forms an integral part of the ninth chapter of this book.
Third Skandha (33 chapters, 1410 verses)
This consists of two long quotations by शुक, of dialogues that took place bet-ween उद्धव and विदुर, and between विदुर and मैत्रेय. It is sometimes interspersed with hymns and remarks by परीक्षित् and शुक.
The story of mutual fighting among the Yādavas and their destruction, the ascension of कृष्ण to his Abode, कृष्ण’s message to विदुर through उद्धव, विदुर’s seeking Self-knowledge from the sage मैत्रेय and the latter’s teaching containing the philosophy of ज्ञान and भक्ति (knowledge and devotion) as taught by कपिल to his मोथेर् Devahūti—are the other contents of this book.
Fourth Skandha (31 chapters, 1431 verses)
This skandha deals mainly with the stories of the daughters of Svāyambhuva मनु (a progenitor of mankind) and their lineage.
The story of destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice due to the wrath of रुद्र who had been antagonized by दक्ष and the episode of the child devotee ध्रुव who retires to the forest and performs auste-rities to gain the grace of Lord विष्णु are the main contents of this book.
Fifth Skandha (26 chapters, 668 verses)
A considerable part of this skandha is in prose.
A schematic description of ब्रह्माण्ड or the universe and detailed description of the earth form an important part of this book. The purpose seems to be to help the devotee to meditate on the physical universe as the body of the Lord.
This skandha also contains the stories of great devotee-kings like Priyavrata, ऋषभ, भरत and others.
There is also an interesting description of twenty eight kinds of narakas or purgatories.
Sixth Skandha (19 chapters, 849 verses)
This skandha starts with the story of अजामिल, a sinner who was saved by uttering the word ‘Nārāyaṇa’ on his death-bed, thereby revealing the mysterious power inherent in the divine name.
Another episode dealt with in detail is that of वृत्रासुर, a fiend who fought with इन्द्र, but was defeated and killed by him. वृत्रासुर was a great devotee of Lord विष्णु. Actually he was a devotee king Citraketu born as a fiend due to a curse.
Seventh Skandha (15 chapters, 750 verses)
Misbehaviour provoking the dis-pleasure of holy persons, results in downfall. On the other hand, pleasing them through devoted service can lead to spiritual evolution. This is the theme developed in this skandha.
The examples given are those of नारद, जय and विजय. नारद had to be reborn as a servant boy of low birth.
Jaya and विजय, attendants of Lord विष्णु at his abode वैकुण्ठ, were reborn as the demons हिरण्याक्ष and Hiraṇya-kaśipu. The story of हिरण्यकशिपु also contains a detailed account of his son प्रह्लाद, one of the greatest exemplars of divine love. प्रह्लाद survives all the attempts of his ड़थेर् to kill him, due to the protection afforded by the Lord विष्णु to whom he had totally surrendered himself. The discourses of प्रह्लाद on the cult of भक्ति, known as the भागवत-धर्म are an important part of this skandha.
There is also a nice description of varṇāśrama-dharmas, ideals of the social system according to castes and stages of life.
Eighth Skandha (24 chapters, 931 verses)
This skandha contains three important incidents: the story of Gajendra, the elephant king; the churning of the ocean of milk and the obtaining of अमृत or nectar by the gods; the story of Mahābali, the king of the असुरस् being vanquished by Lord विष्णु as वामन (the Dwarf).
This skandha also gives the details of the manvantaras or epochs of मनुस् (patriarchs endowed with divine powers).
The last part of skandha deals with naimittika-प्रलय (intermediary deluge) that occurs at the end of a day of ब्रह्मा, the Creator and the मत्स्यावतार (Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्).
Ninth Skandha (24 chapters, 964 verses)
Dealing mainly with genealogies of the great kingly and priestly lines, this skandha also gives accounts of some eminent personalities from among them.
First comes the story of the sage च्यवन, his मर्रिअगे with Sukanyā (daughter of king Śaryāti), her devoted service to the old sage and the blessings of the twin gods अश्विन्स् upon the couple.
Then comes the story of king अम्बरीष, a great devotee of Lord विष्णु, how the sage दुर्वासस् wanted to harm him and how he was protected by the सुदर्शन-चक्र, the Discus of the Lord विष्णु.
Another notable episode is that of the king रन्तिदेव who had gifted away everything and was living a very austere life. Once, after a long period of religious ड़स्तिन्ग् when he was about to take his ड़ोओद्, he readily parted with it to feed hungry guests.
The stories of the kings ययाति, दुष्यन्त and his wife शकुन्तला as also the story of the Pāṇḍavas are the other episodes that appear in this section.
Tenth Skandha (90 chapters, 3946 verses)
This is the biggest book of the Bhāgavata and is generally divided into two parts: the Pūrvārdha (the first part) consisting of 49 chapters and 2005 verses; the Uttarārdha (the second part) comprising 31 chapters and 1941 verses. It deals with the story of Śrī कृष्ण in great detail.
The birth, childish pranks and exploits of Lord कृष्ण during his childhood days, his play with the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvan, his journey to मथुरा along with his elder brother बलराम, his killing of the tyrant कṁस, the ruler of मथुरा, his एदुचतिओन् under the sage सान्दीपनि, his marriages with several princesses, his innumerable conquests as also his helping the Pāṇḍavas in various ways have been dealt with in detail.
Eleventh Skandha (31 chapters, 1366 verses):
The main topic of discourse in this skandha which is the concluding part of the कृष्ण saga, is मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence. The teachings of the Navayogīs or the nine sages to Vasudeva containing the भागवत-धर्म and कृष्ण’s long discourse to उद्धव, now well-known as the Uddhavagītā, are the main contents of this book. The Uddhavagītā deals mainly with spiritual values like holy association, supremacy of devotion and details of the four yogas or paths to enlightenment.
The book ends with the mutual destruction of the Yādavas and the exit of कृष्ण from this world.
Twelfth Skandha (13 chapters, 566 verses)
This is practically the prologue to the whole work.
The genealogy of kingly lines that ruled after कृष्ण’s ascension, the importance of devotion to God in कलियुग and the last part of the story of परीक्षित् are the main contents of this book. A synopsis of the whole Bhāgavata and the ceremonial way of studying it have been added at the end.
KṚṢṆA
Sage व्यास composed the Bhāgavata solely to express his devotion to the Lord by describing his glory through the कृष्ण इन्चर्नतिओन्. Hence no study of the book can be complete without touching upon कृष्ण, the person and the personality, his doings and sayings.
The Bhāgavata declares that कृष्ण is God himself, ‘kṛṣṇastu भगवान् svayam’ (1.3.28). Since God is perfect, कृष्ण, his human manifestation, too is perfect. His physical form and beauty are highly bewitching. His speech is exceedingly sweet. His intellect and wisdom, shrewdness and farsightedness, are matchless. His strength and power, valour and heroism are simply awesome. But, he is not a tyrant, though tyrants quake on hearing his very name. His heart is as soft as the butter he loves to consume in liberal quantities. A friend of the lowly and the meek, compassion incarnate, he is the first to rush to protect those in distress. Destroyer of demons, conqueror of emperors, he makes and unmakes kings, himself never accepting a throne. Wealth and power come rolling to his feet unasked, but he is most detached towards them.
Kṛṣṇa is as great a spiritual preceptor as he is a warrior. Lord of योग and goal of the yogīs, his teachings as given to the गोपीस् or उद्धव, reveal the rarest of insights, but are intensely practical.
Kṛṣṇa’s dealings with the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvan are often cavilled at, without a careful scrutiny. The king परीक्षित् himself raises serious doubts about कृष्ण’s (appa-rently) unwholesome doings. शुक’s reply which sets his doubts at rest, runs on these lines: Even the sages who have gone beyond the bonds of कर्म due to spiritual enlightenment got by meditating upon the feet of the Lord, are beyond the dos and don’ts of धर्म. Then what to speak of him who is born out of his free will to save mankind? Sometimes these great ones act, transgressing धर्म, but with a higher purpose. In such cases their words, and not actions, should be emulated. For instance, शिव drank the deadly poison हालाहल to save the worlds. We cannot do so. अग्नि or fire can consume anything that is cast into it. We cannot.
In whichever way the devotees approached कृष्ण, in the same way did he respond. He knew that the गोपीस्’s love was tainted with sex-passion. Like an expert psychiatrist he responded to it, in order to draw it out from the subconscious levels and destroy it, himself remaining all the while unaffected (vide 10.33.26). That this technique worked, is shown by the fact of their realizing him as their very Self (10.47.53).
Born in a prison, he liberates others from prisons and bondage. Brought up by the cowherds he is highly admired and respected even by great sages and mighty kings. Though subjected to all kinds of tyranny, he frees others from tyranny and fear. He is an ideal householder, an ideal man of renunciation, a hero of thousand battles who knows no defeat, the terror of despots and hypocrites, a master statesman, a consummate man of action, a friend of the lowly ones including the untouchables—he is all things to all persons and hence, ‘Puruṣottama,’ the Best of Men.
PHILOSOPHY OF THE BHĀGAVATA
The Bhāgavata is a gospel of divine life and love, and not a treatise of philosophy. It is based upon विज्ञान, the direct experience of the Reality but includes ज्ञान (rational philosophy built on it) also.
According to it, ब्रह्मन् or आत्मन् is the only absolute Reality. The whole universe is only an expression in name and form of this Reality. Other terms used to indicate it are: परमात्मन्, Pratya-gātman, पुरुषोत्तम, अक्षर, तुरीय, भूमन् and so on, as in the उपनिषद्स्. But the Bhāgavata calls it also by such other names as कृष्ण, वासुदेव, नारायण, Hari and so on. It is however pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, beyond words and thought and free from all limitations.
The Bhāgavata accepts four प्रमाणस् or valid sources of knowledge: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference), āptavākya (tradition of spiritual experience of saints) and śruti (Vedas). However, all these can only point to ब्रह्मन्, but cannot give direct experience.
The work describes ब्रह्मन् as an impersonal Super-person, the creator, sustainer and final refuge of the world of matter and मिन्द्. He is present in every atom of the universe in all his glory. Māyā is the infinite power he wields. He takes whatever form his devotees desire to worship him in, continuing to remain formless too. The emphasis in the text is more on personal God with form, as more suited to love, devotion and worship. And, कृष्ण is God himself; or, rather, God is कृष्ण himself !
‘Bhagavat’ is one of the central concepts of the text. The word ‘Bhagavān’ frequently used both for the personal God and the Absolute, means the ‘gracious Lord,’ ‘the Adorable One’. It is also used as a term of respect while referring to saints and holy men.
Then comes the concept of ‘avatāra,’ God come down (avatāraṇa = coming down) as a living being, in order to help mankind to rise to divine levels by restoring the spiritual equilibrium. The Bhāgavata refers to several avatāras, there being no uniformity in the number or sequence, which varies from ten to forty.
The Bhāgavata also refers to the four ‘Vyūhas’ or emanations from Lord विष्णु. They are sometimes classed under avatāras though considered as different from avatāras that arise as a response to certain cosmic situations. They are: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध. They are different aspects of manifestation of the six qualities known as ‘bhaga’ (like ज्ञान or knowledge, बल or power, ऐश्वर्य or lordship and so on). While वासुदेव has all the six qualities in full measure, the other three have two each in greater measure than the others.
The Ṛgvedic concept of ‘Puruṣa’ also can be seen here. He is the Cosmic Person manifesting himself objectively as the individual and the universe. He is also called ‘Puruṣottama’ and कृष्ण is पुरुषोत्तम.
Then comes māyā, the power of God. It has three guṇas or strands, सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्. The whole universe is a product of the permutation and combination of these three when their equilibrium is disturbed by the will of God, who himself remains inactive like a magnet, itself at rest, inducing movement in iron filings.
The world process appears to the devotees of the Lord as only his ‘līlā’ or sport. He takes pleasure in it, the redemption of the struggling souls being its main purpose.
The most important aspect of the teachings of the Bhāgavata is the mode of sādhanā it prescribes for attaining perfection. भक्ति, love or devotion, has been given the pride of place, though ज्ञान (knowledge), योग (contemplation) and कर्म (right activities) too find an important place in its scheme. भक्ति has been advocated as a more natural and hence an easier, path to perfection.
Bhakti has two aspects. When undertaken as the preliminary discipline, it is called ‘sādhanā-भक्ति’ or ‘vaidhī-भक्ति.’ It is more of the nature of कर्म or activities like worship or chanting or singing the divine names or other rituals. This ripens into ‘aikāntikī’ or ‘ahaitukī’ or ‘ātyantikī’ (intense, single-pointed) भक्ति, wherein love flows unobstructed towards God even as a river flows into the ocean. It is also termed as ‘nirguṇā भक्ति.’ One who has attained to this state of intense devotion is called a ‘mahābhāgavata’ (a great devotee of God) or ‘bhāgavatottama’ (the best of devotees).
The object of भक्ति may be the personal God or an अवतार, or the whole universe. Of these, भक्ति towards an अवतार is the easiest and the sweetest. This भक्ति can take several forms depen-ding upon the relationship that the devotee cultivates towards the Deity: śānta (peaceful contemplation), dāsya (servitude), vātsalya (parental love), sakhya (friendship) and kānta or mādhurya (conjugal love).
Sometimes, even hatred and fear of God have been included within the orbit of भक्ति by the text, since the intense concentration brought about by them on God can purify and liberate them that do so.
Since love naturally expresses itself as service of the loved ones, the Bhāgavata lays great stress on service of the Personal God or saints or even the beings of the world as God’s manifestation. Service to the poor, the needy and the suffering is especially advocated.
Another peculiar feature of the work is the special reverence it advises one to cultivate towards the मोथेर्-land. भारतवर्ष, named after the great राजर्षि (sagely king) भरत, is not a mere geographical unit but the मोथेर् of civilization and, the very embodiment of moral and spiritual culture.
There is a fairly detailed treatment of the subject of varṇāśrama-धर्म (scheme of duties according to castes and stages of life) which is a vindication of man’s right to grow to the heights of spiritual realization. Character and conduct, rather than birth, are recognized as the sine qua non of greatness. It is also stressed that devotion helps one to transcend the limitations. imposed by birth.
Religious emotion leads to reverence which expresses itself as worship. The Bhāgavata deals with ritualistic worship also as a part of the practice of devotion. Worship of pratimās (icons) and pratīkas (symbols), the sun, holy rivers like the गङ्गा and the Himālaya mountains are mentioned as aids to devotion. It is also stressed that the devotee should never pray to God for anything for himself since the omniscient God knows what is best for him.
The highest goal of life is called मुक्ति. It is a state of freedom from all bondage and getting back one’s natural state of divinity or bliss. भक्ति and जप (repetition of God’s name) are the most efficacious means of purifying the मिन्द् leading ultimately to मुक्ति.
It is interesting to note that the work considers भक्ति as the fifth puruṣārtha or value of life, beyond the other four, including even मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. भक्ति is not merely the purifying agency, a means for a higher end, as in the view of many monistic thinkers, but, as its highest, is the acme of life, transcending मुक्ति.
Though several varieties or aspects of मुक्ति such a sārūpya (having a form similar to that of the Lord) or सालोक्य (living in the world of God, viz., वैकुण्ठ) are described, Bhāgavata is more inclined towards parābhakti, the highest or the most intense love of God, as the goal of life, wherein a semblance of the duality between the devotee and the Deity is kept up.
Following the usual traditions of the पुराणस्, the Bhāgavata also deals with many concepts involving immense time-periods and almost boundless regions of space in its narrations about च्रेअतिओन्. They become intelligible and meaningful only when it is recognized that the पुराणस् trace the origin of the universe to the Supreme Being and accept the cyclic theory of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and withdrawal as against the linear theory held by the modern scientists. Thus, they deal with cosmic history and geography.
LITERARY GRACE
The Bhāgavata is also a work of exceptional literary merit. It is as graceful as it is tough. Whether it is a description of nature (10.20) or of places like मथुरा and द्वारका (10.41; 10.37) or depiction of the well-known navarasas (nine poetic sentiments—10.29; 10.60; 10.37; 10.8; 10.80, 81), Bhāgavata excels in every way. No wonder then, that the community of scholars have, for centuries, accepted it as a touchstone of their erudition.
TRADITIONAL COMMENTARIES
For this very reason, the Bhāgavata has attracted the attention of several scholars who have composed commentaries on it. As many as 44 commentaries are known to exist.
By far, the Bhāvārthadīpikā of श्रीधरस्वामिन् (14th cent.) seems to be the most popular of these commentaries. Brevity and clarity, a rather difficult combination, are its chief characteristics. It has also steered clear of controversies. Dīpinī is sub-commentary on this work by Rādhāramaṇadāsa Gosvāmin. Since Śrīdhara was a monk of the Advaita school of Vedānta, the other two schools—Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita—did not want to lag behind. The Bhāgavata-candrikā of Vīrarāghavācarya and the Padaratnāvalī of Vijayadhavaja-tīrtha are the commenta-ries, respectively, of these two schools. The other well-known commentaries still holding their sway among the followers of the respective cults are: Subodhinī of Vallabhācārya (A. D. 1473-1531); Siddhānta-pradīpa of Nimbārkā-cārya (12th cent.); Kramasandarbha of जीवगोस्वामिन् (15th cent.) and Sārārtha-darśinī of Viśvanātha-चक्रवर्तिन् (17th cent.). Sanātana Gosvāmin (15th cent.) has chosen to comment only on the tenth skandha. This work, Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣiṇī, is highly venerated by the followers of the चैतन्य school.
CONCLUSION
The Bhāgavata is essentially a devotional text. Much of the metaphysics found in it is theological in nature, supporting the devotional doctrines. The metaphysics, however, is that of Vedānta. Hence, the ideas stated in the उपनिषद्स् are often found here, sometimes using the very words or expressions. Though the work leans heavily towards advaita, the supre-macy of the Personal God, especially as नारायण or Mahāviṣṇu or कृष्ण, is always upheld; so also भक्ति or devotion to him as the best means of achieving anything in life.
However, the भक्ति advocated here is not sentimentalism. It is upāsanā or meditation brought about by वैराग्य (renunciation) and ज्ञान (knowledge of the Reality). Even sentimental devotion can help since it is directed towards the Lord, who knows how to react, correct, lead and guide his devotees.
Attempts have also been made in the work to reconcile the शिव and the विष्णु cults, at loggerheads with each other at that time.
Synthesis of the paths of ज्ञान, भक्ति and कर्म is another feature noticed here.
But the greatest achievement of the Bhāgavata is the projection of the कृष्ण saga and the कृष्ण personality in the most poetical, and yet, powerful and graceful language. If कृष्ण remains as the darling of millions of Hindu hearts even today, it is not a little due to this matchless work.
